name: Christian Anarchism
summary: Christian anarchism holds that Jesus' teaching, above all the Sermon on the Mount's call to non-resistance and love of enemies, is incompatible with the state, which rests on violence and claims an allegiance owed only to God. Adherents are overwhelmingly pacifist, reject war, oaths and military service, favour voluntary poverty, sharing and servant leadership, and distrust hierarchical churches. Methods are nonviolent: refusal, civil disobedience and community, not revolution or politics.
scope: The mainstream pacifist strand: Tolstoy (The Kingdom of God Is Within You, drawing on Ballou, Garrison and Chelcicky), Jacques Ellul (Anarchism and Christianity) and the Catholic Worker tradition of Dorothy Day and Ammon Hennacy. Excludes violent Christian revolutionary movements and non-anarchist Christian socialism. Many answers on modern issues are low-confidence inferences because the sources focus on the state, violence and property.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Ellul calls money the domain of Mammon, and the movement favours sharing goods over competition, so markets are not credited with superior allocation; they distrust government equally.

public-ownership.rationale: State ownership would enlarge the violent state they consider illegitimate; they prefer voluntary sharing and community.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Ballou's catechism, reproduced by Tolstoy, says Christians should not voluntarily pay taxes yet not resist them, so they would not call on the state to tax anyone; they urge the rich to give voluntarily.

unions-good.rationale: Adherents split: Catholic Worker figures backed labour solidarity, while others reject organised coercive pressure; the sources do not settle it.

property-fundamental.rationale: Helchitsky as reported by Tolstoy says a Christian cannot even be a landowner, and the early church shared goods; property is not a right to be protected by force.

cut-welfare.rationale: They would not defend state welfare as such, but cutting aid to the poor contradicts Jesus' teaching on charity; they want it replaced by voluntary giving, not simply abolished.

surveillance-ok.rationale: They reject state violence and its security justifications, and refuse ends-justify-means reasoning.

strong-leader.rationale: Ellul holds the state illegitimate and concentrated authority hostile to Christian freedom; Jesus' model is servant leadership.

state-harmful.rationale: Ellul says the state is illegitimate and must be destroyed unless it serves all; Wikipedia describes the state as violent, deceitful and idolatrous in their view.

limit-guns.rationale: They are pacifists who reject owning arms for violence, but oppose state coercion to disarm; adherents are split.

empower-police-military.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is not about military spending, which this statement now asks about alone.

reviewHistory.rationale: Tolstoy calls on Christians to refuse military service, and they reject state violence entirely.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is not about military spending, which this statement now asks about alone.

decide-locally.rationale: They prefer horizontal, small-scale, voluntary human relations over hierarchy, which favours local decision.

rehabilitation.rationale: Love of enemies and forgiveness reject retribution; Tolstoy argues government force cannot suppress evil.

traditional-family.rationale: Adherents divide; the movement's sources focus on nonviolence and the state, not family structure.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Christian anarchists are divided on the underlying ethics while generally opposing state control of marriage.

abortion-legal.rationale: Many Catholic Worker-linked adherents oppose abortion, others do not; they split and the state's role is rejected anyway.

more-religion-public.rationale: They oppose state-church alliance since Constantine; Christianity should be lived, not backed by public power, though they are devout.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Tolstoy lists renouncing national distinctions among Christian commands; they hold that all mankind are countrymen.

gradual-change.rationale: They reject deference to state institutions, though Ellul prefers persistent small refusals over sudden revolution; so not respecting institutions outweighs.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Garrison's declaration endorsed by Tolstoy: our country is the world; state border enforcement is state violence.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Any larger government is still a human government to which Christians give no allegiance.

nation-first.rationale: Tolstoy renounces national distinctions and patriotism as contrary to Christ's teaching.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Military action is rejected even to resist evil; non-resistance is central.

open-borders.rationale: Our country is the world; they reject the state's authority to bar people.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: No documented position; the state-led form would be rejected, while stewardship is accepted.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Ellul was a leading critic of technique and its domination of human life.

revolution-justified.rationale: Violent revolution is rejected; Garrison called the spirit of Jacobinism one of retaliation and murder.

central-planning.rationale: Central planning is state power; Ellul says the state is illegitimate unless it serves all.

land-value-tax.rationale: A tax is state coercion; Helchitsky doubted landownership but the tax solution is not their programme.

tax-inheritance.rationale: They do not advocate state taxation, though Ballou's catechism accepts non-resisting taxes.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Nationalist economic policy contradicts renouncing national distinctions.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Increases state power, which they consider illegitimate.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Dorothy Day's distributism is compared to Proudhon's mutualism, but others favour communal sharing; split.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Ellul calls money the domain of Mammon, but abolition is not a programme for most adherents.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: State-recognised bodies are state machinery; they reject.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Christian anarchists cite the Old Testament demand for a king as a fall into coercive authority and see all rulers as non-binding.

democracy-best.rationale: Ballou's catechism says taking part in elections is participation in government by force; they do not see democracy as a legitimate authority either.

direct-votes.rationale: They reject voting as participation in force, yet horizontal decisions in communities are valued; split.

natural-rulers.rationale: They hold God alone as authority and favour servant leadership and horizontal relations.

political-violence-never.rationale: Most are pacifists who reject violence even in response to violence and hold that ends never justify means.

war-builds-character.rationale: War is condemned as incompatible with Christ's teaching.

separate-church-state.rationale: They condemn the Constantinian union of church and state as corruption, so separation is favoured, though they see the state as illegitimate anyway.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Tolstoy reads the Sermon on the Mount as a rule for personal conduct and rejects coercive law, so scripture is not to be made state law; the cited sources do not take up the question directly.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Garrison's declaration says Christians cannot sue at law and all violent defence is rejected.

military-superiority.rationale: Tolstoy condemns the arms race that is exhausting the European states and says each man called up should refuse to serve in the army at all.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Renouncing national distinctions; all mankind are countrymen.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Ellul broke with Marx and rejects violent struggle; Christian love is the alternative.

civilizational-union.rationale: Rejects political unions based on identity; allegiance only to God.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Ellul calls money Mammon's domain and the movement stresses selflessness, servant leadership and voluntary poverty.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Duty to God and neighbour is central, but no community-over-individual state demand.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Ellul criticised technique, but Tolstoy and Day have milder or different views.

algorithmic-government.rationale: More state and technique, both opposed.

restore-past-order.rationale: They see the Constantinian church-state order as a corruption; but they look back to the early church.

results-over-ideology.rationale: They hold that ends never justify means and follow Christ's commands as principle.

direct-action.rationale: Hennacy and O'Reilly favoured nonviolent civil disobedience; Ellul says challenging power is the means of freedom.

means-match-ends.rationale: Wikipedia reports the view that the ends never justify the means; nonviolence in pursuit of a loving community.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Voluntary simple living is admired but not foraging.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Early Christian communities shared goods; Catholic Worker hospitality reflects it, voluntarily.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Ellul notes the bourgeoisie used Christianity to subjugate workers, but there is no explicit labour theory.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Ellul says absolute freedom conquered becomes dictatorship; they reject coercive rule.

collective-farming.rationale: Voluntary communal farming appeals but not as a mandated rule.

taxation-theft.rationale: Ballou's catechism says not to pay taxes voluntarily but not to resist collection; they don't call it theft.

harm-principle.rationale: They deny state restriction at all, yet moral law is stricter than harm principle.

conscription.rationale: Tolstoy calls on Christians to refuse military service and examines compulsory service as evil.

state-as-business.rationale: They reject both state and commodified relationships.

organic-representation.rationale: They reject representation in government by force.

total-state.rationale: Ellul writes that political authority by its essence tends to grow without limit and become totalitarian, and must meet a radical negation from Christians.

national-rebirth.rationale: Tolstoy and Ellul reject nationalism and patriotism as idolatry of the state, so a call for national rebirth runs against them, though neither discusses the statement's decadence-and-rebirth theme.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Tolstoy calls patriotism a savage superstition and quotes with approval the call to renounce conquests as veritable crimes against humanity.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Tolstoy opposes oaths of allegiance and Jesus' ban on oaths.

universal-morality.rationale: Christ's teachings are held to apply to all people, as in Tolstoy's commands.

rule-by-example.rationale: Servant leadership and moral example over coercion fit their view.

national-self-determination.rationale: Tolstoy renounces national distinctions, so national states are not a right.

force-without-un.rationale: Tolstoy holds that Christ's law of non-resistance forbids any part in war, so no authorisation, international or otherwise, could make force abroad acceptable.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Faith in Christ's teaching is foundational.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: All mankind are countrymen; charity does not discriminate by nationality.

class-collaboration.rationale: Love of enemies and nonviolence favour cooperation over struggle.

ban-interest.rationale: They reject state prohibition; Mammon critique applies though.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Ellul says the bourgeoisie used Christianity and the state to subjugate workers.

proportional-representation.rationale: Participation in elections is itself rejected.

national-mission.rationale: Tolstoy treats every government as organised violence and patriotism as a superstition taught to keep people obedient, so no nation has a mission to spread its rule.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The state is seen as violent and deceitful, and rulers' authority is not binding.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: State control over who may have children is coercion, and the tradition holds every person of equal worth; no cited source discusses eugenics.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: They reject state justice systems yet condemn killings.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The state is held illegitimate, even minimal.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: A core of Christian teaching and servant relations; stated in Garrison's declaration of mankind.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: They reject state law as authority.

consent-of-governed.rationale: They deny any human government's claim, with or without consent.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Pacifism rejecting violence even in response to violence.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: They oppose state coercion over political belief.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Ellul says the state is illegitimate unless it serves all; they reject domination.

separated-powers.rationale: Still government; they reject it though less than concentrated power.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Core of Jesus' teaching, Catholic Worker hospitality for the poor.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Opposes state coercion against nonviolent protest.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Contradicts Christian view of institutions and greed.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: They reject offices by the sources I read, so this is a low-weight inference from their anti-state, nonviolent principles.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The ends do not justify means.

party-controls-media.rationale: Ellul reads the beast from the sea in Revelation as political authority that perfectly symbolizes political propaganda, which Christians are to refuse.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Opposes binding oaths and obedience to human authority.

church-by-bishops.rationale: The strands differ: Tolstoy was excommunicated and rejected church hierarchy, and Ellul says institutionalised love produces authority and hierarchy, while Dorothy Day's Catholic Worker accepted the authority of the Catholic bishops.

clerical-rule.rationale: Ellul condemns the church's theology of the state since Constantine and the Christian authoritarianism of later centuries, and reads Jesus' stance toward political authority as radically negative.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: They refuse war service but reject violent defeatism; split.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: They don't take part in elections.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: State prohibition opposed; they favour sharing housing voluntarily.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Tolstoy admired peasant life; the sources used do not centre it.

death-penalty.rationale: Garrison and Quakers rejected capital punishment, as noted by Tolstoy; love of enemies.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: They oppose state schooling imposing religion.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Moral concern but state coercion opposed; split.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Duty to the poor is universal; voluntary.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Early Christians shared goods; property is conditional.

collective-defense.rationale: Tolstoy dismisses alliances and balance-of-power schemes as no road to peace and asks instead whether each man should serve in the army at all, answering that he should not.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Rejects state but not specifically addressed.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Tolstoy and Ellul reject the state's authority over religious life as much as any other authority, so placing churches under state control is opposed, even though both are also critical of the institutional church.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Rejects heads of state by the sources I read, so this is a low-weight inference from their anti-state, nonviolent principles.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Tolstoy and Ellul treat reverence for rulers as idolatry and hold that God alone has authority, which rejects a sacred head of state.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Still government by the sources I read, so this is a low-weight inference from their anti-state, nonviolent principles.

leader-cult.rationale: Idolatry rejected; God alone is authority.

land-redistribution.rationale: Violent seizure opposed, though Helchitsky doubted landownership.

refugee-return.rationale: Opposes state barriers by the sources I read, so this is a low-weight inference from their anti-state, nonviolent principles.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Ellul holds the state illegitimate and rejects strengthening it for any cause; revolutions end in greater enslavement.

moral-incentives.rationale: Tolstoy and the Catholic Worker urge voluntary poverty, sharing and service from conscience instead of profit.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Non-resistance and love of enemies are central; Tolstoy rejects all violence including revolutionary violence.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Ellul and Tolstoy reject hierarchy and rank as contrary to Jesus' teaching of servant leadership and equality.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Rule of one people by another rests on violence, which Christian anarchists reject, and Tolstoy condemned it as hypocrisy.

patriotic-education.rationale: Tolstoy attacked patriotism and drilling children in national loyalty as contrary to Christ's teaching and a tool of state power.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Sources critique money and property but offer no theory of capitalist collapse; indifferent.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Nationalist and imperial ambition is a form of state violence and idolatry in Tolstoy's and Ellul's view.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its own rationale argues against its value: it accepts nonviolent resistance, which the statement now covers, yet gives a negative.

reviewHistory.rationale: Non-resistance to evil is central to Tolstoy's reading of the Sermon on the Mount, so removing a ruler by force is rejected; disobedience remains allowed.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its own rationale argues against its value: it accepts nonviolent resistance, which the statement now covers, yet gives a negative.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Voluntary poverty, sharing and servant leadership are central, and the Sermon on the Mount commands care for the poor.

native-born-offices.rationale: Tolstoy's critique of patriotism and nation is central to his argument against state allegiance.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Rejection of war and patriotic claims is central to the Christian anarchist position.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: They oppose fascism but place no faith in state constitutions.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Tolstoy rejects military service and war, so a political role for armed forces is rejected.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Voluntary poverty, sharing and the rejection of mammon are core Christian anarchist themes, and Ellul treats money as a power opposed to God.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Non-resistance and love of enemies are the core of the doctrine, and Tolstoy rejects all state violence and war.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Tolstoy and Ellul reject military force by states and the use of troops against others, whatever the justification.

democratic-peace.rationale: Ellul and Tolstoy treat all states, democratic or not, as resting on violence, so spreading democracy is not a path to peace.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Tolstoy argues allegiance is owed to God, not the state, and refuses oaths and obedience to commands that conflict with Jesus.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Love of enemies and rejection of nationalism rule out blaming a minority for a conspiracy.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Tolstoy rejects patriotism and national sovereignty as a claim on conscience, so national precedence is not accepted.

religious-nation.rationale: Tolstoy and Ellul reject patriotism and tie the Kingdom of God to no nation, so a creed-defined nation is refused.

religion-illusion.rationale: Faith in Jesus' teaching is central, so religion as a mere illusion is rejected.

treaties-binding.rationale: Adherents distrust state authority but value keeping one's word; they do not address such treaties.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Voluntary sharing and communities like the Catholic Worker houses are central, though not all hold property in common.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Tolstoy and Ellul reject the state's violence and coercion as such, including its use to silence dissent, and call for nonviolent resistance to it.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Tolstoy argues that church and state have used violence to enforce belief against Jesus' teaching of non-resistance, so punishment of blasphemy by civil government is rejected.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Tolstoy condemns governments' wars and exploitation for the benefit of ruling classes, and the tradition rejects state power in general, so colonial rule for economic gain is rejected.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Christian anarchists reject armed overthrow of rulers as strongly as rule itself, holding that violence cannot establish a godly order; Tolstoy insists on non-resistance even to evil governments.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Adherents oppose domination of every kind but the tradition does not use the intersectional framework, and its focus on the state, violence and property leaves the claim neither endorsed nor rejected.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: The tradition says little on this, and modern Christian anarchists differ between compassion for trans people and traditional views, while rejecting state coercion either way; adherents are split.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Christian anarchists place themselves outside state politics and both left and right as Ellul and Tolstoy describe them, but the claim that the best ideas of each should be combined is an inference.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Nulled (Codex review, 2026-11-10): the statement now asks only whether political authority ultimately comes from God, no longer "rather than from the people". This answer weighed divine origin against the people (or treated moral authority as political authority), which the new text no longer sets against each other; its sources need re-reading.

reviewHistory.rationale: Christian anarchists hold that only God holds legitimate authority and reject the state's claim to it, but they deny that this makes any human government legitimate, so agreement with the statement is qualified.

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (Codex review, 2026-11-10): the statement now asks only whether political authority ultimately comes from God, no longer "rather than from the people". This answer weighed divine origin against the people (or treated moral authority as political authority), which the new text no longer sets against each other; its sources need re-reading.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Tolstoy says Christians must refuse military service and Ellul and the Catholic Worker reject war, so abolishing armies is central to the tradition.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Christian anarchists reject all earthly rulers and hereditary kingship as a claim to an allegiance owed only to God (Tolstoy, Ellul read 1 Samuel 8 as a rebuke of monarchy).

racial-franchise.rationale: Their universal love and Tolstoy's rejection of patriotism and national distinctions oppose limiting political rights by race, and they reject the state's franchise anyway.

open-government-data.rationale: They reject the state, so the question of how it should handle records is not one they address; secrecy is disliked but they do not seek to improve government.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Their rejection of coercive state law and their universal-love ethic oppose legal limits on whom adults may marry.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: The command to love one's enemies and Tolstoy's rejection of national and religious enmity oppose shunning people by their faith.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Ellul and the Catholic Worker treat the pursuit of wealth as service to Mammon and favour sharing and voluntary poverty, so accumulations of money are seen as corrupting power.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Faith is a matter of conscience, and a state forcing belief or unbelief is exactly the coercion they reject; Tolstoy and Ellul oppose state control of religion.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Tolstoy rejects violent punishment and coercive government, and they favour nonviolent community means of dealing with wrongdoing; most adherents would still not call for abolition by political action.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Voluntary hospitality and mutual aid among believers, as in the Catholic Worker, is their model for helping the poor in place of the state.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Tolstoy treats military training and drilling for the state as incompatible with Christ's teaching.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Voluntary poverty and sharing, and Ellul's critique of property, favour rewarding work over mere ownership.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Tolstoy's Kingdom of God Is Within You rules out killing even to resist evil, including in defence of others.

municipal-property.rationale: Christian anarchists favour sharing and voluntary community of goods, but the sources do not decide on municipal ownership.

person-over-state.rationale: Ellul and Tolstoy hold that obedience is owed to God and conscience, not the state, and that no person may be used as a means by it.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Christian anarchism is grounded in the spiritual life and teaching of Jesus, with material concerns subordinate.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Tolstoy rejects patriotism and national divisions as contrary to Christian brotherhood, and the same reasoning rules out racial blocs.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Tolstoy's non-resistance rejects all military service and violence, including war in defence of the country.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Christian anarchists owe allegiance to God alone and reject nationalism; Tolstoy condemns patriotism and national divisions as contrary to Christ's teaching.

arms-reduction.rationale: They oppose war and armies and call for refusal of military service, so reduction agrees with their aim though its 'national safety' premise is not theirs.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Christian anarchists reject the state as an institution resting on violence, so granting it a monopoly of arms is firmly opposed.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Tolstoy's Kingdom of God Is Within You makes refusal of military service and of war central, and the movement is overwhelmingly pacifist.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Methods are nonviolent refusal and community, not revolution or politics, so smashing the state is not their route even though they deny its legitimacy.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: They favour sharing and simple living but have no stated view on economic pluralism; adherents split.

sacred-nation.rationale: Tolstoy rejects patriotism as a form of idolatry, since allegiance is owed only to God.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Debt forgiveness has biblical echoes, but they would not look to the state for it; adherents split.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: The Sermon on the Mount's non-resistance and love of enemies rule out holding weapons of mass killing; Tolstoy rejects all military force.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Tolstoy and Ellul condemn state courts and punishment, and the Sermon calls for forgiveness; fixed state penalties are rejected.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Adherents hold the Sermon on the Mount to be binding and plain, but reject church orthodoxy and read scripture critically; the strands split.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Christian anarchists reject war and refuse to defend any state, and see state power as violence claiming loyalty owed to God.

national-church-status.rationale: Tolstoy and Ellul condemn the alliance of church and state, and the churches' privileged legal status as a betrayal of Jesus.

simple-living.rationale: Voluntary poverty and sharing are core, as in Tolstoy's later life and the Catholic Worker.

equal-conscription.rationale: Christian anarchists reject military service for anyone, so the 'or to neither' reading matches their view and men-only conscription is rejected.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Non-resistance and love of enemies rule out killing anyone, let alone without trial.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Ellul and Tolstoy reject Christian involvement in politics and state-church alliances, so politics organised by denomination is opposed.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Christian anarchism has no documented position on technology versus ancestral tradition; adherents are split between simple living and acceptance of technology.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Christian anarchists hold that God's law binds above the state's, so obeying God rather than human commands makes unjust law void in conscience.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Tolstoy condemns patriotism as idolatry of the state and a cause of war, so tying it to any politics is rejected.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Christian anarchists reject the state and party rule as claims on allegiance owed only to God.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: They would not defend state welfare as such, but cutting aid to the poor contradicts Jesus' teaching on charity; they want it replaced by voluntary giving, not simply abolished. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

former-empire-equal-treatment.rationale: Nationalist and imperial ambition is a form of state violence and idolatry in Tolstoy's and Ellul's view. (Carried over from former-empire-influence, "A country should cultivate political and cultural influence in regions once ruled by its predecessor empire.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: A person should refuse to serve in the armed forces even when the law requires it.
missingStatements.rationale: Tolstoy says the Christian's duty is to refuse meekly but firmly to serve in the army.

missingStatements.text: Sworn oaths of allegiance to the state or its officials are wrong.
missingStatements.rationale: Tolstoy and Ballou read the Sermon's ban on oaths as forbidding binding oaths and allegiance oaths.
missingStatements.declined: Narrow to Christian and a few pacifist traditions (Quakers, Anabaptists); few other ideologies in the bank would take a side, so it would not separate ideologies.

missingStatements.text: Citizens should not take part in government by voting or holding office.
missingStatements.rationale: Ballou's catechism, reproduced by Tolstoy, calls participation in election and government participation in force; Hennacy and others abstained, though not all adherents agree.

notes: Ellul read Romans 13 as a reason not to overthrow the state, while Hennacy and O'Reilly favoured civil disobedience; strands differ on voting, taxes and the Church. Only part of the long Wikipedia and Tolstoy texts was read.
